title: The Dangerous Lives of Altar Boys
full_review:
Two high school boys devise a nasty scheme to exact revenge on their Catholic school teacher with catastrophic results in the disturbing drama "The Dangerous Lives of Altar Boys" (ThinkFilm).

Directed by Peter Care, this adaptation of the late Chris Fuhrman's novel is a story about adolescent angst and anger aimed at the Catholic Church, the authority figure in the two boys' lives. Originally slated to premiere at Sundance 2000, the coming-of-age story, set in the South in the 1970s, was pulled from the lineup to allow more time to develop the film's animated sequences. Created by Todd McFarlane, the animation reflects the inner fantasies as well as the real life events of best friends Francis (Emile Hirsch) and Tim (Kieran Culkin), who feel they are suffering greatly under the strict regulations of their icy Catholic school teacher, Sister Assumpta (Jodie Foster, who also produces). Chaffing under her rules and daily efforts to subvert their fun instead of the genuine concern she has for their souls, the boys channel their aggression into a coarse comic book that depicts one-legged Sr. Assumpta as Peg Leg, a fiendish, motorcycle-riding villain who battles their animated super hero alter-egos.

When the comic book lands in the hands of Sister Assumpta, who seems to be one of only two staff members at the whole high school, Francis and Tim plot a far-fetched scheme to recover their sketchbook that will also rid them of Sr. Assumpta. It is clear that their plan, which involves a cougar, can only end badly.

In the meantime, Francis is experiencing first love with Margie (Jena Malone). But the innocence of first love is shattered when Francis discovers that Margie harbors a desperate secret from her past: incest. By introducing this issue, the film catapults the young characters into a mature world they are ill-prepared to handle, but must manage nonetheless. Up to this point, the film has made it clear that the boys' enemy is the repressive Catholic Church, as represented by Sr. Assumpta. Their rebellion and hostility is aimed at her. But the introduction of this very upsetting situation shows that some of the faith teachings Sr. Assumpta drilled into them have sunk in. Francis doesn't hesitate to forgive Margie, he simply does. Whether or not he understands what he is doing, Francis embraces the core of what it means to be Catholic by loving Margie, faults and all, unconditionally.

Hirsch is natural and convincing as Francis, who is the story's linchpin. He taps into the Francis' sensitivity without turning him into a sap. Despite knowing that Tim's revenge plan is reckless and dangerous, Francis goes along with it. He understands that Tim, whose contributions to the comic book cannot compete with those of Francis', needs to feel he has accomplished something. Yet despite the fine development of these characters, the film doesn't draw the viewer into their troubled world. The story gives very little in the way of atmospherics to understand why the boys would rebel in such a vicious manner, other than their own capriciousness.

The audience is meant to understand that the boy's home lives, particularly Tim's, are terrible although this is inadequately sketched. Despite the title, the boys are seen assisting at Mass only once, and their own feelings on religion or faith are never fleshed out, which makes the setting of a Catholic school more of an afterthought than a pointed dig. There is the feeling that these boys would not have acted differently had they been in a public school.

Another problem with the film is the representation of underage drinking. In several of the scenes, Tim, Francis and their two other friends are seen guzzling beer or any liquor they can get their hands on and when they happily smoke marijuana, it is shown as desirable. The boys suffer no repercussions from either the alcohol or the substance abuse.

Foster is disappointing in the stern, authoritarian role. She is unable to balance the spiritual and disciplinarian missions Sr. Assumpta has. Her Irish brogue, which is laid on thickly in initial scenes, all but disappears in subsequent ones. Vincent D'Onfrio plays an ineffectual priest whose role as the school is unclear.

The animated sequences are razor-sharp, clearly depicting the relationship between the live-action and the cartoon scenes. However, the transition from the boys' misadventures to their animated heroic deeds is often jarring, and the long stretches between the cartoon sequences requires the viewer to think back to where the animated story line had last left off.

"The Dangerous Lives of Altar Boys" means to be an affecting story of the difficulties of adolescence, but ultimately fails to deliver the powerful punch of which it initially seems capable. The inclusion of the serious theme of incest and the narrative's tragic conclusion result in a disjointed but nonetheless somber film.

Due to graphically animated depictions of a violent nun, brief realistic violence, sporadic sexual references including incest, recurring underage drinking, brief drug use and intermittent rough language, profanity and crass expressions, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R- restricted.

- - -

Navarro is on the staff of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Office for Film and Broadcasting.
